title: The Good Shepherd (Statue, Museo Pio Cristiano)
date: Late 3rd–early 4th century (reworked as a statuette in 1764)
location: Museo Pio Cristiano, Vatican Museums, Vatican City
summary: A youthful, beardless shepherd in a short belted tunic, leggings and boots, with a satchel at his side, carries a lamb across his shoulders, holding its legs in his hands and gazing calmly outward. The figure was originally carved in high relief on a sarcophagus decorated with pastoral scenes, found in the Catacomb of Callixtus on the Appian Way, and was cut free and completed as an independent statuette in 1764. Though much restored, this gentle figure is one of the best-loved images of early Christian Rome, giving almost three-dimensional form to the image that dominated Christian art before Constantine: Christ the shepherd who goes after the lost sheep and carries it home rejoicing.
facts: It entered the papal collections in 1764, when it was sold for the Christian Museum of Pope Benedict XIV; the restorers of that time recarved or replaced parts of the head, the arms, one leg, the lamb's legs and the back.
The museum that houses it today was founded by Pope Pius IX in 1854 to preserve finds from the Roman catacombs that could not be kept in their original sites.
The pose follows the ancient Greek 'kriophoros' (ram-bearer) type, a figure long associated with Hermes; Christians adopted it with new meaning.
Early Christians largely avoided free-standing statues, which were associated with pagan cult images; the shepherd's origin as a sarcophagus relief reflects this preference for relief carving.
The shepherd's short tunic is the working dress of a Roman herdsman, not royal or priestly robes: Christ is shown as one who serves.

title: The Brescia Casket (Lipsanoteca)
location: Museo di Santa Giulia, Brescia, Italy
medium: Carved ivory on a wooden frame (with a later silver lock plate)
summary: This small ivory box is covered with finely carved scenes from both Testaments, with the life and Passion of Christ at its heart: Christ teaching, healing, raising the dead, praying in Gethsemane, and standing before his judges. Throughout, Christ appears as a beardless, long-haired young man of serene authority, a type favoured in fourth-century Italy. Made probably in Milan in the time of Saint Ambrose, it is one of the richest surviving cycles of early Christian narrative art.
facts: Its Italian name, 'Lipsanoteca', means reliquary, but it may originally have been made as a casket for other precious objects and only later used for relics.
Christ's Passion is shown without the Crucifixion itself, typical of the period, when artists still avoided depicting the cross with Christ upon it.
Old Testament scenes, such as Jonah and Daniel, appear alongside the Gospel episodes as prefigurations of salvation and resurrection.
In the nineteenth century the casket was taken apart and its panels displayed flat on a cross-shaped board; it was restored and reassembled as a box only in 1928.
commons: File:Museo di Santa Giulia Santa Maria in Solario lipsanoteca Brescia (cropped).jpg

title: The Crucifixion and the Death of Judas (Maskell Ivory)
summary: On a small ivory panel from a casket of Passion scenes, Christ hangs on the cross, alive, upright and open-eyed, beneath the inscription REX IVD[AEORUM], 'King of the Jews', while the Virgin, Saint John and the soldier with the spear stand nearby. To the left, Judas hangs lifeless from a tree, his bag of silver spilled at his feet. Together with the doors of Santa Sabina, it is among the very earliest surviving narrative images of the Crucifixion, and its contrast of the two deaths, one defeated and one triumphant, is a profound meditation on the cross.
facts: The panel is one of four from the same casket, which together show Pilate washing his hands, Peter's denial, Christ carrying the cross, the Crucifixion, the empty tomb and Thomas touching the wounds.
Christ is shown not slumped in suffering but heroically alive, with a strong, athletic body, a way of showing victory over death that would dominate Crucifixion images for centuries.
The panels are known as the 'Maskell Ivories' after William Maskell, the collector and writer on ivories from whom the British Museum acquired them in the nineteenth century.
The tree from which Judas hangs bears a bird feeding its young, often read as a sign of the new life that springs from Christ's death.
commons: File:Ivory plaque of the Crucifixion of Christ.jpg

title: The Adoration of the Magi (Triumphal Arch, Santa Maria Maggiore)
location: Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore, Rome (in situ)
summary: High on the triumphal arch of Rome's great basilica of the Virgin, the infant Christ sits alone on a wide, jewelled throne, attended by angels, while the Magi in Persian dress approach with their gifts. Rather than a baby in his mother's arms, he is shown as a small sovereign receiving homage, an image of the incarnate Word as King from the first moment of his earthly life. The arch's cycle of Christ's infancy is among the earliest surviving monumental sequences of its kind.
facts: The mosaics were made under Pope Sixtus III (432–440), whose dedication 'XYSTUS EPISCOPUS PLEBI DEI' ('Sixtus, bishop, to the people of God') still appears at the top of the arch.
The programme is closely linked to the Council of Ephesus (431), which proclaimed Mary 'Theotokos', the God-bearer, to defend the full divinity of the child she bore.
Mary appears beside the throne dressed like a Roman empress, and a second dignified female figure on the other side has been interpreted variously as a personification of the Church or a Sibyl.
The arch also includes rarely depicted episodes, such as the Holy Family's meeting with Aphrodisius, governor of an Egyptian city, drawn from apocryphal tradition.

title: Christ in Glory (Vision of Ezekiel), Hosios David
location: Church of Hosios David (Latomou Monastery), Thessaloniki, Greece (in situ)
summary: In the small apse of a Thessaloniki church, a young, beardless Christ sits on a rainbow within a luminous circle of glory, holding an open scroll of praise and surrounded by the four living creatures, while two prophets gaze up at him in awe from the banks of the rivers of Paradise. It is a vision of the Lord's appearing, drawn from Ezekiel and the Book of Revelation, and among the finest early Byzantine mosaics to survive. An inscription below the scene speaks of the church as a life-giving spring that receives and nourishes the souls of the faithful.
facts: A Byzantine legend says the mosaic was hidden under an ox-hide and mortar to protect it from iconoclasts, and later miraculously revealed; it was rediscovered in the early 20th century beneath Ottoman-era plaster.

The church served as a mosque during the Ottoman period and was reconsecrated as an Orthodox church in 1921, when it came to be called after Saint David the Dendrite; its original dedication is uncertain, perhaps to Christ the Saviour.
The two prophets are usually identified as Ezekiel and Habakkuk (some propose Isaiah), who recorded visions of God's glory.
Since 1988 the church has formed part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Paleochristian and Byzantine Monuments of Thessaloniki'.
commons: File:Thessaloniki Church of Hosios David fresco.jpg

title: The Barberini Ivory
medium: Carved elephant ivory, originally set with precious stones (seven pearls survive)
summary: An emperor, usually identified as Justinian, rides in triumph at the centre of this splendid five-part ivory, while conquered peoples bring tribute and Victory hovers beside him. Yet the highest place belongs to Christ: at the top, a youthful Christ blessing is borne aloft in a medallion by two angels, flanked by the sun, moon and a star. The composition is a statement of Byzantine political theology, in which all earthly victory flows from, and is subordinate to, the heavenly ruler.
facts: It is one of the finest surviving pieces of Byzantine ivory carving and the best-preserved example of a five-part imperial ivory leaf; one of its five plaques is lost and was replaced by a later board.

On its back, a seventh-century hand wrote a list of names, including Frankish kings of Austrasia, showing that the ivory had reached Gaul early and was used in the liturgy to record those to be prayed for.
It takes its name from Cardinal Francesco Barberini, who received it in 1625 from the French scholar Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc; the Louvre acquired it in 1899.
Christ's gesture of blessing above the emperor mirrors the presentation of tribute below, placing the earthly court under heaven's authority.
commons: File:Ivoire Barberini - Musée du Louvre Objets d'art OA 9063 ; MND 211.jpg

title: The Antioch "Chalice"
location: Metropolitan Museum of Art (The Cloisters Collection), New York, USA
medium: Silver (inner cup); silver with gilding (outer shell and foot)
summary: An openwork cage of gilded grapevines encloses a plain silver cup, and among the vines sit twelve figures: two images of Christ, the others variously identified as apostles or as ancient sages who foretold his coming. Birds, a lamb, snails and other small creatures fill the branches, evoking Christ's words 'I am the vine; you are the branches'. Once sensationally claimed to be the Holy Grail itself, it is now valued as a superb work of early Byzantine silverwork.
facts: It was reportedly found near Antioch around 1910, and when it was first published in 1916 the plain inner cup was proclaimed to be the cup of the Last Supper.
It was exhibited as the Holy Grail at the 1933 Chicago World's Fair, and was acquired for The Cloisters in 1950.
Its shape has more recently been identified with that of standing lamps used in sixth-century churches, which is why the Metropolitan Museum places 'Chalice' in quotation marks.
The vine-scroll imagery recalls both the Eucharist and the Gospel of John's image of Christ as the true vine.

title: Christ of the Second Coming (Apse of Santi Cosma e Damiano)
location: Basilica of Santi Cosma e Damiano, Roman Forum, Rome (in situ)
summary: Against a deep blue sky streaked with fiery sunset clouds, a majestic, bearded Christ in golden robes descends as if walking down a staircase of cloud, his right hand raised, while Saints Peter and Paul present the physician-martyrs Cosmas and Damian to him, joined by Saint Theodore and Pope Felix IV. It is one of the most dramatic apse mosaics of Rome, an image of the Lord's return in glory set above the old Roman Forum. Its monumental, almost tangible Christ became a model for Roman apses for centuries.
facts: Pope Felix IV (526–530) created the basilica in 527 from buildings of the ancient Forum of Peace given by the Ostrogothic rulers Theodoric and Amalasuntha; it is often called the first church in the Roman Forum.
Below the main scene, twelve lambs approach the Lamb of God on a hill from which the four rivers of Paradise flow, symbolising the apostles and the faithful.
The phoenix perched on the palm tree at the left is an ancient emblem of resurrection.

The figure of Pope Felix holding a model of the church is largely the work of later restorers, and the arch was cut down in the 17th-century rebuilding, but the central composition is essentially sixth-century work.
commons: File:Church of Cosmas and Damian, apse mosaic in the Roman Forum.jpg

title: The Transfiguration Cross (Apse of Sant'Apollinare in Classe)
location: Basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe, Ravenna (in situ)
summary: Rather than a human figure, the apse presents the Transfiguration through symbols: a great jewelled cross set in a starry blue disc, with a tiny bust of Christ at its centre, flanked by Moses and Elijah, while three sheep below stand for Peter, James and John. Beneath, Saint Apollinaris, Ravenna's first bishop, prays among his flock in a green paradise of trees and flowers. It is a subtle and luminous image of Christ's hidden glory revealed through the cross.
facts: Above the cross is the Greek word IXΘYC ('fish'), an acrostic for 'Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour'; below it is the Latin 'SALUS MUNDI', 'Salvation of the world'.
The hand of God emerges from the clouds at the top, recalling the voice from heaven at the Transfiguration.
The basilica was consecrated in 549 by Archbishop Maximian, the same bishop whose ivory throne survives in Ravenna.
It is one of eight early Christian monuments of Ravenna inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.
commons: File:Basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe - Mosaic.jpg

title: Christ before Pilate (Rossano Gospels)
location: Museo Diocesano e del Codex, Rossano, Calabria, Italy
medium: Tempera, silver and gold on purple-dyed parchment
summary: On a page of purple-dyed parchment, Pontius Pilate sits on his tribunal, flanked by imperial standards bearing portraits of the emperor, while Christ stands calmly before him and the crowd presses in. Painted with the immediacy of a theatre scene, it belongs to one of the oldest surviving illustrated Gospel books in the world. The page sets the dignity of the accused Christ against the machinery of imperial justice.
facts: Purple parchment was associated with imperial luxury, and the Greek text of the manuscript is written in silver and gold ink.
A companion page shows the crowd choosing between Christ and Barabbas, a rare early depiction of that moment.
The manuscript was brought to scholarly attention in 1879 by the German scholars Oscar von Gebhardt and Adolf von Harnack.
In 2015 it was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

title: Tapestry Icon of the Virgin and Child, with Christ in Glory
location: Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, Ohio, USA
summary: Woven entirely in coloured wool, this large hanging shows the Virgin Mary enthroned with the Christ child on her lap, flanked by the archangels Michael and Gabriel; above them, Christ appears in a radiant glory supported by two angels. A border of medallions portrays the apostles, each named in Greek. One of the very few textile icons to survive from the early Byzantine world, it joins the incarnate child and the glorified Lord in a single, prayerful image.
facts: Egypt's dry climate preserved this fragile textile, while countless painted and woven icons elsewhere perished, including during the iconoclast controversy.
The composition borrows from Byzantine imperial art: Mary is enthroned like an empress among her court officials, here the archangels.
At nearly 1.8 metres tall and woven from more than twenty colours of wool, it was a costly object, made to hang on a wall as an icon for veneration.
The Cleveland Museum of Art acquired it in 1967; the museum notes that in its own day such a tapestry cost more than a painted icon.

title: The Communion of the Apostles (Stuma Paten)
created: Constantinople (silver stamps of Justin II); found at Stuma, Syria
summary: On this silver liturgical plate, Christ appears twice behind an altar: on one side he gives the consecrated bread, on the other the cup, to apostles who come forward with reverently bowed heads. The scene shows the Last Supper not as a historical meal but as the heavenly liturgy, with Christ himself as the celebrant of every Eucharist. The paten would have held the bread during the Divine Liturgy, so that the image and the sacrament met on the same surface.
facts: Official control stamps on the back date the silver to the reign of Emperor Justin II (565–578).
It was found in the early twentieth century at Stuma in northern Syria, and scholars have associated it with the group of village church silver known as the Kaper Koraon Treasure.
A near-twin, the Riha Paten, is at Dumbarton Oaks in Washington, D.C.; both were gifts of donors to Syrian village churches.
The 'Communion of the Apostles' became a standard subject for the apses of Byzantine churches, directly above the altar.

title: Pilgrim's Ampulla with the Crucifixion and Ascension
location: Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, Ohio, USA
summary: Small enough to sit in the palm of a hand, this flask once held oil blessed by contact with the holy places of Jerusalem, and was carried home by a pilgrim as a precious souvenir. Its front shows the Crucifixion and its back the Ascension, with Christ enthroned in glory above the apostles. Such humble, mass-produced flasks preserve images that may echo the great lost mosaics of the Holy Land's churches, and they shaped how Christians everywhere pictured these events.
facts: It belongs to the same 'Monza/Bobbio' type as the famous Monza ampullae, which Queen Theodelinda of the Lombards gave to Monza Cathedral around 600 and which are still kept in its treasury.
On ampullae of this kind the Crucifixion is often shown with Christ's bust above the cross rather than his body upon it, a reticence typical of the period.
The oil inside was taken from lamps burning at shrines such as the Holy Sepulchre, and was believed to carry the blessing of the place.
Only a little over fifty such ampullae are known to survive, making them a crucial source for early Christian iconography.

title: The Alexamenos Graffito
artist: Unknown (a pagan scratching on a wall)
summary: Scratched into the plaster of a room on the Palatine Hill, a crude figure with the head of a donkey hangs on a cross, while a young man raises his hand toward it; the Greek caption reads, roughly, 'Alexamenos worships [his] god'. It was made to mock a Christian, perhaps a page boy in the imperial household. Yet this scorn is often called the oldest surviving image of Jesus, and it is the earliest known picture of the crucifixion: before Christians themselves dared to depict the cross, a scoffer drew it — and in doing so bore witness to the faith he ridiculed.
facts: It was discovered in 1857 in the domus Gelotiana, a building on the Palatine that served as a school (paedagogium) for imperial page boys, and was later cut from the wall for preservation.
In a neighbouring room a different hand wrote 'ALEXAMENOS FIDELIS' — 'Alexamenos is faithful' — perhaps a friend's reply, or Alexamenos's own.
Early Christian writers, among them Tertullian and Minucius Felix, record the slander that Christians worshipped a donkey's head; this graffito is that slander in pictures.
Its date is debated, with proposals from the late 1st to the late 3rd century; around AD 200 is most widely accepted.

title: The Baptism of Christ (Crypts of Lucina)
location: Crypts of Lucina (double chamber X–Y), Catacomb of Callixtus, Via Appia, Rome (in situ)
summary: On a pale, damaged wall two red-brown figures meet at the water's edge: a tall, clothed man at the right reaches out his hand to a smaller, naked figure who climbs up out of the water, while at the upper left a dove flies down towards them. It is the Baptism of Christ by John, with the Spirit descending as a dove, painted in a few quick strokes. Made around AD 200 in the oldest part of the Catacomb of Callixtus, it is one of the very earliest surviving pictures of any event in the life of Jesus.
facts: Wilpert, who published it in 1903 (plate 29), recorded the scene above the door to cubiculum Y of the double chamber in the Crypts of Lucina, the earliest nucleus of the Catacomb of Callixtus; the same pair of rooms holds Daniel among the lions, two Good Shepherds, Jonah and the famous 'Eucharistic' fish with baskets of bread.

The official guide to the Catacombs of St Callixtus (A. Baruffa) dates the paintings of this double chamber to the end of the 2nd century; others place them in the early 3rd, so a date around 200 is usually given.

As in almost all early images of the Baptism, Christ is shown small, young and naked, standing in the water beside a larger Baptist – a convention that underlines the humility of the Son of God and recalls the nakedness of early Christian baptism.
